parsed_answer.content: Sorting and searching form the bedrock of algorithmic efficiency in Java development. Binary Search is the quintessential divide-and-conquer strategy for searching, requiring a pre-sorted array to achieve O(log n) time complexity by halving the search space per iteration. Merge Sort is a stable, divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that guarantees O(n log n) performance in all cases by recursively splitting the array and merging sorted subarrays, though it incurs an O(n) space complexity penalty due to auxiliary array allocation. Quick Sort, conversely, is an in-place sorting algorithm that typically performs faster in practice due to better cache locality, though it suffers from a worst-case O(n^2) time complexity if the pivot selection is poor (e.g., already sorted data with a fixed pivot). When dealing with a rotated sorted array—an array that was originally sorted but shifted at an unknown pivot index—we must adapt the Binary Search logic. By checking which half of the array is sorted (the left or the right) during each step, we can determine if the target lies within the sorted range or the rotated range, maintaining the O(log n) efficiency.

items: Binary Search on rotated arrays relies on the invariant that at least one half of the array (left or right of the midpoint) must be sorted at any given time.
Merge Sort's stability makes it the preferred choice for sorting objects in Java where maintaining the relative order of equal elements is required, such as in custom Comparator implementations.
Quick Sort's worst-case O(n^2) is mitigated in production environments by using a randomized pivot or the 'median-of-three' rule to avoid degenerate partitions.
In JVM memory management, Merge Sort's O(n) space requirement can trigger frequent Young Gen GC cycles if sorting large arrays, whereas Quick Sort's in-place nature is more memory-efficient.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Engineer Insight: Always watch for integer overflow when calculating the midpoint. Using 'mid = (left + right) / 2' can overflow if the array size exceeds 2^30. Always use 'mid = left + (right - left) / 2' to ensure safety in production-grade systems.
